P16g: I still don’t know how to keep this language of capacity from becoming a respectable way to exclude people who are disabled, poor, less articulate, unfamiliar with therapeutic language, or simply inconvenient. Pretending capacity is unlimited won’t solve that. Any real process would need concrete criteria, review by someone who wasn’t part of the decision, and a way to revisit a “not now” decision. Even then, the power to veto membership applications based on capacity remains dangerous.
P12s: The problem is that, in a group of eight people, if two are in a sustained crisis mode, the group may end up spending most of its attention caring for those in crisis. However, in a group of eighty people, the same need, or even more of it, can often be spread across lots of relationships and roles. A group can only absorb as much need as its members have free resource to meet.
P22n: Any humane membership process should have ways of not flat-out rejecting people who fall into these categories, like saying “later,” or “in another role,” or “with more support.”
P13q3: Welcoming someone is partly a question of resources, then, not compassion -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they are taking in?
P13q4: The ability to welcome somebody is partly a problem of resources, then, not compassion -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they are taking in?
P3g: So the question isn’t whether a person is “good enough” for community. The practical question is how much attention they currently have available for other people, how willing they are to examine their own reactions, and whether the group has enough capacity to support them without being consumed.
P6g: That does not make the community infinitely absorbent.
P14p4: So early on, members usually need to have more available resource than acute need, and some practical skills to contribute, and a willingness to learn.
